deadjectival -e adverb.mapping_rationale: Wright §§552-553 treat ordinary adverbs formed from adjectives, especially adverbs in -e, such as sōþe 'truly', hearde 'fiercely', wide 'widely', and rihte 'rightly'. Old English Online likewise gives -e as one of the common adverb-forming endings.

deadjectival -līce adverb.mapping_rationale: Wright §553 explains that adverbs like cræftlīce, dōllīce, frēondlīce, and gelīce arose from adjectives in -līc, after which -līce was reanalyzed as an adverbial ending. Old English Online also gives -līce as a major adverb-forming suffix.

-unga / -inga adverb.mapping_rationale: Wright §554 treats adverbs in -inga, -unga, -linga, and -lunga, such as dearnunga/dearninga 'secretly', eallunga/eallinga 'entirely', færunga 'suddenly', and grundlunga 'to the ground, completely'. Old English Online also identifies -unga as a common adverb-forming suffix.

-linga / -lunga adverb.mapping_rationale: This is a subtype of the -unga/-inga adverb group in Wright §554. It is useful as a separate implementation subtype because -linga/-lunga forms are visually distinct and often lexicalized.

regular comparative / superlative adverb.mapping_rationale: Wright §555 treats regular comparative and superlative adverbs, generally with -or and -ost, e.g. hearde/heardor/heardost and holdlīce/holdlīcor/holdlīcost. Old English Online describes the same pattern as dropping final -e and adding -or and -ost.

irregular or i-mutated comparative / sup.mapping_rationale: Wright §556 treats adverbs with older comparative -iz and superlative -ist/-ost formations, including eaþe/ieþ/eaþost, feorr/fierr/fierrest, lange/leng/lengest, and softe/seft. Old English Online likewise lists i-mutated and irregular adverb comparison types.

suppletive comparative / superlative adv.mapping_rationale: Wright §556 also includes adverbs whose comparative and superlative come from a different stem, such as wel/bet/betst, lȳt/lǣs/lǣst, micel/mā/mǣst, and yfele/wiers/wierst. These should be lexeme-specific in an annotator.

case-form adverb.mapping_rationale: Wright §557 says a large number of OE adverbs consist of cases of nouns and adjectives used adverbially. This is one of the most important historical categories for tagging because many look like ordinary inflected noun/adjective forms.

degree adverb.mapping_rationale: This is a semantic tag rather than a Wright morphological class. Wright lists degree-like adverbs such as swīþe 'exceedingly, very', micel/micle 'much', ungemete 'excessively', and full 'very, perfectly'. For an annotator, degree adverb should probably be a semantic subtype layered on top of formation type.

negative adverb.mapping_rationale: Negation is not one of Wright's §§552-558 adverb-formation classes, but for annotation it is important to tag ne, nā, nō, nāwiht/nōwiht and similar forms as negative adverbs or negative particles. I would model this as a semantic/function tag rather than a formation class.
